questions.question: What is pattern matching in Ruby 3?
questions.title: Pattern Matching in Ruby 3
questions.direct_answer: Pattern matching (Ruby 3.0, stabilized 3.1) lets you destructure and branch on shape: `case expr; in {name: String => n, age: 18.. => a}; ...; end`. `in` matches + binds; `=>` binds a sub-pattern to a name. Common: array `in [a, *rest]`; hash `in {status: 'ok', data:}` (data: binds :data); type `in Integer`; range `in 1..100`; guard `in Integer => n if n.odd?`. The `=>` (rightward assignment, 3.0) puts a value into a variable: `result => {status:, data:}`. `in` raises NoMatchingPatternError if nothing matches (use `else` for a fallback). Use it for parsing JSON/API responses, branching on event shapes, and replacing deep if/elsif. It's expressive but read-only in `case/in`; for destructure-with-bind, prefer it over nested dig/[].

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know pattern matching (Ruby 3.0+) uses `case/in` to destructure + bind on shape (array/hash/type/range).
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using `when` instead of `in` (case/in, not case/when), or forgetting `else` (NoMatchingPatternError if no match).
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Pattern matching (Ruby 3): case/in destructures + binds on shape (array/hash/type/range). `=>` binds. No match -> NoMatchingPatternError (use else).

sections.title: Destructure and Branch
sections.content: Pattern matching (Ruby 3.0, stabilized 3.1) lets you destructure and branch on shape: case expr; in hash name String n age 18 dot dot a dot dot dot end. in matches and binds; the right-arrow binds a sub-pattern to a name. Common: array in a rest; hash in status ok data (data binds the data key); type in Integer; range in 1 to 100; guard in Integer n if n dot odd. The rightward assignment (3.0) puts a value into a variable: result right-arrow status data. in raises NoMatchingPatternError if nothing matches (use else for a fallback). Use it for parsing JSON/API responses, branching on event shapes, and replacing deep if elsif. It's expressive but read-only in case in; for destructure with bind, prefer it over nested dig or square brackets.

sections.title: Pattern Matching
sections.content:
case/in destructures + binds. `=>` binds. No match -> NoMatchingPatternError (else).

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  C[case expr] --> I[in {status:'ok', data:}]
  I --> B[bind: data = the data key]
  I --> A[in [a, *rest]]
  I --> T[in Integer]
  M[no match] --> E[NoMatchingPatternError; use else]
```

sections.title: Pattern matching
sections.content:
```ruby
# Ruby 3.0+: pattern matching with case/in (NOT when)
case { status: 'ok', data: [1, 2, 3] }
in { status: 'ok', data: }          # binds `data` to [1,2,3]
  puts data                        # [1, 2, 3]
in { status: 'err', message: }    # alternative pattern
  puts message
else
  raise 'unknown'
end

# Array patterns:
case [1, 2, 3]
in [a, *rest]                       # a=1, rest=[2,3]
  puts "first=#{a}, rest=#{rest}"
end

# Type + range + guard:
case 42
in Integer => n if n.odd?           # type-bind + guard
  puts 'odd int'
in 1..100
  puts 'in range'
end

# Rightward assignment (=>, Ruby 3.0): put a value INTO a var
hash => {status:, data:}            # status=..., data=...

# JSON / API parsing (common use):
resp = JSON.parse(body)
case resp
in {status: 'ok', data: [first, *]}
  handle(first)
in {status: 'err', error:}
  raise error
else
  raise 'unexpected'
end

# `in` raises NoMatchingPatternError if NOTHING matches -> use `else`.
```
